name: hybrid-cloud
context: Organizations combining on-premises infrastructure with public cloud services to balance workload placement based on regulatory, latency, cost, and scalability requirements. Hybrid-cloud architecture integrates private cloud, public cloud, and on-premises datacenters into a unified distributed computing environment, enabling workloads to run where they make most sense economically and operationally.
benefits: Workload placement flexibility: Run each workload where it makes most sense economically and operationally
Gradual migration path: Enable incremental cloud adoption without big-bang rewrites
Regulatory compliance: Keep sensitive data on-premises to meet data residency and sovereignty requirements
Elastic capacity on-demand: Burst to cloud during peak loads without permanent overprovisioning
Risk management: Avoid putting all infrastructure in a single cloud or location
Cost optimization: Convert CapEx to OpEx and leverage cloud elasticity for variable workloads
Leverage existing investments: Maximize value from existing on-premises infrastructure
Business continuity: Use cloud as disaster recovery site without duplicating all infrastructure
tradeoffs: Network complexity: Additional latency, reliability, and management overhead for cross-environment connectivity
Data consistency challenges: Syncing data across environments with varying consistency guarantees
Operational overhead: Managing two distinct platforms simultaneously
Security surface expansion: Consistent policy enforcement across multiple trust zones
Skill requirements: Teams need expertise in both cloud and on-premises technologies
Hidden costs: Egress fees, data transfer, and dual management can erode cloud savings
Integration complexity: API interfaces needed to connect legacy systems with cloud-native services
Governance fragmentation: Different tooling and processes across environments
use_cases: Regulatory data residency requirements forcing sensitive data to remain on-premises
Gradual migration of legacy applications to cloud with API integration
Cloud bursting for seasonal demand spikes (e-commerce, retail, gaming)
Disaster recovery as a service using cloud for elastic site replication
Edge computing extension where cloud services extend on-premises to remote locations
SaaS integration extending on-premises ERP/CRM with cloud AI/analytics services
Development and test environment provisioning in cloud while production stays on-prem
Cross-border expansion without building new datacenters
avoid_when: All workloads can run in public cloud without regulatory or latency constraints
Team lacks expertise to manage both on-premises and cloud environments
Application requires constant low-latency communication between services across environments
Tight deadlines where establishing hybrid connectivity would slow delivery
Simple workloads where pure cloud or pure on-prem would be significantly cheaper
Organizations ready to fully commit to cloud-native without legacy constraints
component_types: VPN Gateway: Encrypted connectivity between on-prem and cloud
Direct Connect: Dedicated physical connection for low-latency, high-bandwidth
Cloud Interconnect: Cloud-provider direct link for enterprise connectivity
Hybrid Storage Gateway: Data tiering between on-prem SAN and cloud object storage
Identity Federation: Centralized identity management across environments
Cloud Management Platform: Unified control plane across environments
Hybrid DNS: Name resolution spanning on-premises and cloud
Backup & Recovery Appliance: Continuous replication to cloud for DR
Network Load Balancer: Distributing traffic across hybrid endpoints
Observability Platform: Unified monitoring and logging across environments
technology_stack: Network connectivity: AWS Direct Connect, Azure ExpressRoute, Google Cloud Interconnect, VPN Tunnel
Compute: AWS Outposts, Azure Stack HCI, Google Cloud Local, VMware Cloud on AWS
Storage: AWS Storage Gateway, Azure File Sync, Google Cloud Storage Transfer Service
Container orchestration: Kubernetes (Rancher, OpenShift), Amazon EKS Anywhere, Azure Arc-enabled Kubernetes
Infrastructure as Code: Terraform, Ansible, Pulumi
Identity: Active Directory, Entra ID, Okta, AWS IAM Identity Center
Monitoring: Azure Monitor, AWS CloudWatch, Google Cloud Monitoring, Datadog, New Relic
Backup: Veeam, Zerto, Druva, cloud-native backup services
Service mesh: Istio, Linkerd (for hybrid Kubernetes clusters)
anti_patterns: Lift-and-ignore: Rehosting applications to cloud without addressing underlying inefficiencies
Cloud spaghetti: Uncoordinated deployment of cloud resources creating chaos
Hidden cloud lock-in: Using cloud-specific services that create dependency on single provider
Inconsistent identity: Separate credentials on each platform enabling lateral movement risk
Data gravity neglect: Moving data without considering where it will be accessed most frequently
Split-brain operations: Separate operational processes for each environment causing drift
Uneven security posture: Strong security in cloud but weak controls on-premises or vice versa
Cost blindness: Failing to track egress fees and data transfer costs eroding cloud savings
Manual synchronization: Hand-coding data sync logic instead of using managed services
Ignoring network RTT: Assuming cloud and on-prem are equally fast for all workloads
design_principles: Unified Management: Use a single control plane (Azure Arc, AWS Systems Manager) to manage both environments consistently
Identity as the Perimeter: Implement zero-trust identity federation so credentials work seamlessly across environments
Data Locality Awareness: Place workloads where data is accessed most frequently to minimize egress costs and latency
Network Isolation by Default: Implement defense-in-depth with private connectivity between environments
Automation First: Use Infrastructure as Code (Terraform, Pulumi) to ensure consistent deployment across environments
Observable Hybrid: Deploy unified monitoring that tracks requests across both on-prem and cloud boundaries
best_practices: Use dedicated connectivity (Direct Connect/ExpressRoute) for production workloads to minimize latency and maximize bandwidth
Implement VPN as fallback for resilience but don't rely on it as primary for high-throughput workloads
Design for network partition tolerance: ensure workloads can operate independently if connectivity is lost
Implement consistent identity federation (Entra ID, Okta) across environments to prevent lateral movement
Apply uniform security policies through cloud management platforms; don't treat on-prem security as separate
Use encryption for all data in transit between environments; never rely on internal network alone
Implement least-privilege access for cross-environment access; regularly audit hybrid permissions
Classify data sensitivity first, then decide placement: don't move data without considering access patterns
Use managed data sync services (Storage Gateway, File Sync) instead of custom scripts
Monitor egress costs continuously: data transfer can quickly erode cloud savings
Implement consistent backup strategies across both environments with regular DR testing
Standardize tooling and processes across both environments to prevent operational drift
Use Infrastructure as Code for all environment changes: no manual configuration
Implement unified observability with correlated metrics across hybrid boundaries
Regular testing of failover and failback procedures to ensure business continuity
